summary: This document describes version 2 of Core Based Trees, a multicast routing protocol that builds one shared distribution tree per group, for use between and within domains. It was published as experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: One shared tree with a big trunk, and every group member hangs off it to get the same news.

questions: what is a shared multicast tree
subtitle: Shared-tree multicast routing with one core router per group.

tldr.problem: Early multicast routing protocols either built separate paths for each source (source-based trees) or required complex coordination across domains; networks needed an approach that built one efficient shared tree per group while remaining suitable for both intra- and inter-domain use.
tldr.mechanism: CBT version 2 designates a single core router as the meeting point for all senders and receivers of each multicast group, routing all data through this core. Routers join the tree by sending JOIN_REQUEST messages that propagate towards the core and are acknowledged, while keep-alive messages maintain the tree and detect failures.
tldr.outcome: CBT was published as Experimental and is now Historic; while the core-based approach proved influential on later protocols like PIM, CBT itself did not see wide deployment, and the protocol was superseded by more standardized alternatives.

today: RFC 2189 is Historic. CBT Version 2 was published as an Experimental protocol in September 1997 and did not achieve widespread deployment. While the shared-tree and core-based routing approach influenced the design of later protocols such as PIM Sparse Mode, CBT itself was superseded by more widely implemented standards. Today, CBT is mainly of historical and pedagogical interest for understanding multicast routing design.

sections.title: Shared Trees and the Core-Based Approach
sections.content:
RFC 2189 specifies Core Based Trees (CBT) Version 2, a multicast routing protocol that builds a single shared distribution tree per group, rooted at a designated core router. Unlike source-based approaches that create separate trees for each sender, CBT uses one tree per group that all senders and receivers attach to, reducing state in the network and simplifying management across domain boundaries.

In CBT, the core router acts as the central meeting point and rendezvous point between sources and group members. A source that is not already on the tree may send data to the core, which encapsulates it and sends it down the tree to all receivers. Receivers join the tree by working toward the core, and once on the tree, can receive data from any sender. The protocol is suited to both intra-domain and inter-domain multicast and does not require that all routers use the same approach.
sections.plainLanguage: In CBT, one special router (the core) is the meeting point for everyone who wants to send or receive in a group. All the routers form branches off this core, like a tree. If you want to join, you send a message toward the core, and once you are connected, you can hear everything everyone sends.

sections.title: Tree Topology and Router State
sections.content:
The CBT tree is formed by routers maintaining parent and child relationships for each group. A router's parent interface is the one on the path toward the core; child interfaces are those through which downstream routers or receivers are connected. When a multicast packet arrives at a router, it is forwarded over all child interfaces except the incoming interface, allowing data to flow from any sender on the tree to all receivers.

The state in each router is group-specific and bidirectional: a confirmed link can carry traffic in either direction. On links that do not natively support multicast (point-to-point or non-multicast networks), the router must store the address of its parent and any child routers. On multicast-capable links, the parent and child information is represented by the local interface addresses over which they are reachable. This state is created when a JOIN_ACK message is received, confirming that the router is now on-tree for the group.

Loops cannot form in a CBT tree because there is only one active core per group, and tree-building scenarios that could create loops are prevented by immediate pruning: if a router's upstream link becomes unreachable, it immediately flushes all downstream branches, forcing them to rejoin individually.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router knows which interface is toward the core (the parent) and which interfaces point away from it toward receivers (the children). When a message for the group arrives, the router sends a copy out all the child interfaces. The tree has only one core, so there is no way to make loops.

sections.title: Joining the Tree
sections.content:
When a host wants to join a multicast group, it sends an IGMP membership report on its local network. A CBT-aware router on that link receives this and, if it is not already on the tree for the group, originates a JOIN_REQUEST message directed toward the group's core router. This message is sent hop-by-hop; each intermediate router that is not yet on-tree forwards it toward the core and caches temporary state recording the downstream interface from which it came.

The JOIN_REQUEST must be explicitly acknowledged. When the message reaches the core router or another router that is already on-tree and receives the join on a non-upstream interface, that router sends back a JOIN_ACK. This acknowledgement travels the reverse path of the join message back to the originating router, establishing the parent-child relationships at each hop. Once a router receives its JOIN_ACK, it adds the interface to its forwarding cache for that group and is now on-tree.

On multi-access links, the routers elect a designated router (DR) using a HELLO protocol. Only the DR forwards multicast joins and responses on the link, preventing multiple branches from forming. However, if the DR is not the best next-hop toward the core, it can redirect the join message unicast to the true best next-hop, preventing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router wants to join, it sends a special message toward the core. That message hops from router to router, each one remembering it came from this direction. When the message reaches the core or another router already on the tree, that router sends back a yes message. The yes travels back, and now all the routers along the path know how to forward traffic for this group.

sections.title: Maintenance and Control Messages
sections.content:
Once a router is on-tree, it maintains its upstream link by periodically sending ECHO_REQUEST keep-alive messages to its parent router. On multicast-capable links, this message is multicast to the all-cbt-routers group (224.0.0.15) unless the sender is the designated router, in which case it is unicast. The parent responds with an ECHO_REPLY containing the list of groups for which the link is a child, allowing both routers to verify that state is consistent.

If the parent router fails to respond to keep-alive messages within a timeout period, the child router sends a QUIT_NOTIFICATION to its parent, then sends a FLUSH_TREE message downstream to tear down its branches. Downstream routers receiving the flush delete their state for the affected group and can rejoin if they still have local members.

When a router no longer has any downstream receivers or routers for a group, it immediately sends a QUIT_NOTIFICATION upstream. This causes the parent to remove the interface from its child list. If no other child routers reply to defend the link by rejoining, the parent eventually quits as well, pruning the tree in the upstream direction. This allows the tree to shrink dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: After joining, routers send regular heartbeat messages up the tree to make sure the parent is still there. The parent sends back a confirmation. If the heartbeat stops, the child knows the parent is dead, tells the parent it is quitting, and tells everyone downstream to stop using this branch. When a router has no one left who wants the group, it tells its parent it is leaving.

sections.title: Senders and Protocol Status
sections.content:
A sender that is not a member of the tree may send multicast data natively on its local network. A CBT-aware first-hop router that receives this data encapsulates it using IP-in-IP and unicasts it to the group's core router. At the core, the encapsulating header is removed and the packet is disseminated down the tree to all receivers in the normal manner. This approach avoids requiring state in the network for non-member senders and prevents data packets from following arbitrary paths.

The core router for a group can be discovered by one of two mechanisms. The bootstrap mechanism (similar to that used in PIM) allows candidate core routers to advertise themselves to a Bootstrap Router (BSR), which periodically announces the set of candidate cores to all routers in the domain. Leaf routers then use a hash function on the group address to select which core to join. Alternatively, leaf routers can be manually configured with core-to-group mappings.

RFC 2189 was published as an Experimental protocol in September 1997. CBT is now Historic; while the shared-tree and core-based approach influenced later multicast protocols such as PIM Sparse Mode, CBT itself saw limited deployment. The protocol has been superseded by more standardized and widely implemented alternatives, though its design remains valuable for understanding multicast routing trade-offs.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone not in the tree wants to send to the group, they send the message to the core, who passes it along to everyone. Routers find out who the core is either by a dynamic election process or by configuration. The protocol was experimental and did not become widely used, but it showed a good way to think about shared trees.
